question.:question/problem: Given that $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ find $\frac{∂g}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $g(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂g}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂g}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂g}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $g$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x}=\frac{1}{x+y},\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}=\frac{1}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂r} & =(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{1}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{r(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{1}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $w(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ find $\frac{∂w}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $w(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂w}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂w}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂w}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $w$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂w}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂x} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }, \\ \frac{∂w}{∂y} & =\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂w}{∂r} & =(\frac{2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +(\frac{2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{{r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2}{r}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)={x}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +0\,(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)=2y-xy,$ find $\frac{∂f}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂f}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂f}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=2-x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂\theta } & =(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )+(2-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta -{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $h(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find $\frac{∂h}{∂r},$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $h(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂r}+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂r} \\  & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +\frac{∂h}{∂y}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $h$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂h}{∂y}=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =-2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂r} & =(2r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -(2r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2r({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =2r\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Given that $q(x,y)=xy,$ find $\frac{∂q}{∂\theta },$ where $(x,y)$ are Cartesian coordinates and $(r,\theta )$ are the corresponding plane polar coordinates.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Applying the multivariable chain rule for the function $q(x,y)$ with two independent variables $r$ and $\theta ,$ where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂q}{∂\theta } & =\frac{∂q}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂\theta }+\frac{∂q}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂\theta } \\  & =-\frac{∂q}{∂x}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{∂q}{∂y}r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $q$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂q}{∂x}=y,\,\frac{∂q}{∂y}=x\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $r$ and $\theta ,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂q}{∂x} & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta , \\ \frac{∂q}{∂y} & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting these into our chain rule formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂q}{∂\theta } & =-(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =-{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$
